candidates.title: Non-Equilibrium Steady States in Nucleosynthesis
candidates.abstract: Steady-state behavior underlies many nucleosynthesis processes in which the population number of nuclei can remain nearly constant despite the rapid nuclear reactions. While existing theoretical descriptions largely focus on established chemical equilibrium, as in nuclear statistical equilibrium (NSE) and quasi equilibrium (QSE), non-equilibrium steady states (NESSs) can form in process-specific approximations such as classical $β$-flow $r$-process. We develop a general framework for describing NESSs in nuclear reaction networks by formulating the steady-state condition as a balance of reaction flows within a reduced linear description of the relevant network subset. We apply the framework to four representative nucleosynthesis scenarios spanning different steady-state regimes: disequilibrium between nucleons and $α$ particles during $α$-rich freeze-out, the classical $β$-flow steady state, the neutrino-assisted $νr$-process, and the fission-cycling phase of the $r$-process. In particular, the fission-cycling scenario is described by a quasi-steady-state (QSS) approximation maintaining the population ratios between two nuclei while not conserving the total number of nuclei. The framework reproduces the characteristic abundance pattern for each case while providing a unified interpretation of the underlying steady-state behavior. The eigenvalue spectrum reveals network structure and characterizes the relaxation timescales of abundance distributions. These results establish a general approach for analyzing nucleosynthesis beyond the condition of chemical equilibrium and provide a foundation for extending graph-based methods to complicated nuclear reaction networks.

candidates.title: Interpreting the $γ$-Ray Emission of the Cygnus X region with a Combined Cygnus OB2 and Cygnus X-3 Scenario
candidates.abstract: The recent detection of high-energy $γ$-ray emission up to PeV energies from the Cygnus X region points to the presence of a PeVatron therein. This region hosts notable candidates such as the Cygnus OB2 association, which may be associated with PeV $γ$-photons detected by the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO). The X-ray binary Cygnus X-3 also lies along the line of sight to the Cygnus X region, and LHAASO has observed modulated PeV $γ$-ray flux from its direction, indicating that its contribution is also non-negligible. Here, we attempt to interpret the $γ$-ray emission of the Cygnus X region using a combined scenario. Assuming a hadronic origin, we consider contributions from Cygnus OB2, Cygnus X-3, and Galactic cosmic rays (GCRs). Our results show that Cygnus OB2 alone, or its combination with the GCR component, is insufficient to account for the multiwavelength observations, whereas including the $γ$-ray emission from Cygnus X-3 naturally explains these observations. This suggests that the $γ$-ray emission from the Cygnus X region has a more complex origin, necessitating a joint consideration of Cygnus OB2 and Cygnus X-3. The expected neutrino flux from hadronic interactions extends into the GeV band and can help reveal the radiation mechanism of Cygnus X-3, underscoring the need for high-sensitivity GeV neutrino observatories.

candidates.title: XRISM view of a featureless cluster Abell 1060: Revealing the advection of a diffuse radio source by ICM motions
candidates.abstract: Abell 1060 is a nearby, dynamically relaxed galaxy cluster hosting the extended radio structure Flying Fox (FF) near its center. We used high-resolution XRISM/Resolve spectroscopy to measure intracluster medium (ICM) motions and velocity dispersion. Spatially resolved analysis reveals a velocity gradient of approximately 100 km/s along FF and enhanced velocity dispersion near the brightest cluster galaxy NGC 3311, suggesting turbulence generated by galaxy-ICM interactions. These results and the compact extent of FF favor fossil plasma supplied by past activity of the brightest cluster galaxy and transported by ICM motions. We also tested whether the measured turbulence could generate or maintain the nonthermal components of FF. For a velocity dispersion of $96.7^{+23.9}_{-24.6}$ km/s and an assumed turbulence scale of 50 kpc, comparable to the Resolve field of view and approximately half the cluster core radius, the turbulent energy flux is approximately $3.49 \times 10^{-28}$ erg cm$^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$. Although this flux may weakly reenergize pre-existing relativistic electrons, the acceleration timescale of approximately 2.5 Gyr exceeds the synchrotron and inverse Compton cooling timescale of approximately 210 Myr. The present turbulence is therefore insufficient to accelerate electrons to high energies. In situ turbulent reacceleration is unlikely to dominate the generation of FF, although it may help maintain fossil electrons supplied by past AGN activity. These results link ICM dynamics to the origin of nonthermal emission and support a time-evolutionary picture of particle acceleration in galaxy clusters.
